title: Spatiotemporal Patterns of the Vegetation‐Atmosphere Decoupling Coefficient Across the Contiguous United States
content:
Abstract

The decoupling coefficient (Ω), a dimensionless metric that quantifies the balance between stomatal conductance (G s ) and aerodynamic conductance (G a ) in regulating evapotranspiration (ET), is key to understanding vegetation-atmosphere interactions, which are fundamental to ecohydrological cycles and ecosystem functioning. However, the spatiotemporal patterns of Ω across different plant functional types (PFTs) and climatic gradients remain poorly understood, particularly in heterogeneous land surfaces under climate change. Here, we quantified Ω at 52 AmeriFlux sites across four PFTs in the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) from 2001 to 2024 and developed a high-resolution Ω modeling framework that integrates eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) with satellite observations and reanalysis data to produce spatially explicit 8-day Ω maps at 0.1° resolution. This framework reveals a significant increasing trend in continental-mean Ω (1.0 × 10−3 yr−1, p < 0.05), indicating progressively weaker vegetation-atmosphere coupling, whereby ET becomes relatively insensitive to G s and increasingly constrained by available energy. We also found that Ω in water-limited regions show highly volatile and asymmetric responses to drought, shifting toward stronger coupling in dry periods and toward stronger decoupling in wet periods, whereas Ω in energy-limited regions remain strongly buffered with a stable coupling state. Our study reveals the spatiotemporal variability of Ω in CONUS, shedding light on the pivotal role of vegetation in modulating water fluxes under shifting climatic regimes and drought stress.
